findings.title: Stop piping unpinned remote install.sh into sh at build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new RUN downloads https://example.com/install.sh with curl -sL (silent, follow redirects) and immediately executes it as root in the image build. There is no checksum, signature, version pin, or content-type check, so the build runs whatever that URL (or any redirect) returns. That is arbitrary remote code in the produced image, which is then copied over and launched via CMD [/app]. The host is IANA's documentation placeholder, not a software distribution channel, so this also cannot perform a legitimate install.

findings.title: Fail the Docker RUN when curl cannot fetch install.sh
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline is `curl -sL … | sh` under Docker's default `/bin/sh -c` (no `set -o pipefail`) and curl is invoked without `--fail`. `-s` hides curl errors. On a transport failure curl writes no stdout and exits non-zero, `sh` reads an empty script and exits 0, and Docker records a successful layer. Callers cannot distinguish 'install ran' from 'download failed; nothing was installed'; the image still gets COPY/CMD and can be published.

findings.title: Do not pipe an unpinned remote install script into sh
findings.whyItBreaks: The new RUN downloads https://example.com/install.sh and executes it as root during `docker build`. There is no checksum, signature, version pin, or vendor-controlled artifact; `-L` follows redirects. Anyone who can serve or redirect that URL (the host, a CDN/DNS takeover, or a 3xx target) gets arbitrary code execution in every built image, and the result is copied into the runtime layers that `CMD ["/app"]` ships.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL … | sh` uses Docker's default `/bin/sh -c` without `pipefail`, and curl is invoked without `--fail`. Pipeline status is `sh`'s status. If curl fails (DNS/TLS/connect), `sh` reads EOF and exits 0, so the layer is cached as success and `COPY app /app` still runs — the image is tagged as built with no install and no error. Without `--fail`, HTTP 4xx/5xx also exit 0 and pipe the error body into `sh`; `-s` hides curl's diagnostics.

findings.title: Do not pipe an unpinned remote script into sh at build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new layer runs `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh`. That fetches and executes whatever the URL returns at build time with no version pin, checksum, or signature, so a compromised or redirected host becomes RCE in the image. `curl` is invoked without `--fail` (`-s` also hides errors), and the pipeline has no `pipefail`, so the RUN exit status is only `sh`'s: a failed download yields empty stdin, `sh` exits 0, and the image is tagged as if install succeeded. An HTTP error body (this host serves HTML, not an installer) is likewise fed to the shell.

findings.title: Don't map Load's ErrMissing to empty string in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value. Exported LoadOrDefault ignores that error and always returns v, so both cases become "". Callers of this public API cannot distinguish failure from a legitimate empty stored value and will treat the fallback as real.

findings.title: Wait for job goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Run sent every j*2 on results before returning, so a caller could treat return as 'all sends done' (including close(results) then range). Head wraps each send in go func and falls out of the loop with no WaitGroup, ctx wait, or other join, so Run returns while sends are still in flight. Close-after-return is then a send-on-closed-channel panic; a buffered read of len(jobs) immediately after return can see a short slice; an undrained unbuffered results channel leaves the goroutines blocked on send after the call has already ended (leak). The j parameter capture is correct; the defect is missing join.

findings.title: Wait for worker goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, each `results <- j * 2` ran in the `Run` goroutine, so every send happened-before `Run` returned. Callers could therefore close `results` or assume all `len(jobs)` values were already in the channel. The new `go func` launches those sends and returns immediately with no WaitGroup/errgroup join, so (1) `close(results)` after `Run` races the workers and can panic on send-on-closed-channel, (2) a process that exits after `Run` can drop unsent results, and (3) delivery order is no longer the jobs order.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run sent every j*2 on results before returning, so a caller could close(results) (or exit) afterward. The new body schedules N goroutines and returns immediately with no WaitGroup/done signal and still ignoring ctx. A caller that closes after Run — the standard producer pattern, including go func(){ Run(...); close(results) }() — races the sends: send on closed channel panics, or the process exits with results never delivered. Concurrent sends also drop the previous in-order guarantee.

findings.title: Restore admin AND same-tenant check in canDeleteRecord
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required both session.isAdmin and session.tenantId === record.tenantId. OR makes two previously denied cases true: (1) isAdmin=true with a different tenantId skips tenant isolation and allows cross-tenant delete; (2) isAdmin=false with a matching tenantId skips the admin gate and allows any same-tenant user to delete any record. That is an authorization bypass on the exported delete predicate (Session/RecordRef both key on tenantId; isAdmin is tenant-scoped, not a platform superuser flag).

findings.title: Require admin AND same tenant to delete records
findings.whyItBreaks: The delete predicate changed from `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` to `||`. Substituting live values: isAdmin=false with matching tenantId now returns true (any tenant member may delete any in-tenant record; isAdmin is ignored). isAdmin=true with a mismatched tenantId now returns true (a tenant-scoped admin may delete another tenant's records). Both cases returned false before this change. Same-tenant membership also makes the isAdmin conjunct redundant, so the only new power isAdmin grants is cross-tenant delete.

findings.title: Restore tenant-admin conjunction in canDeleteRecord
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported delete gate changed from session.isAdmin && same-tenant to session.isAdmin || same-tenant. Two previously denied cases now return true: (1) isAdmin=false with matching tenantId — any tenant member may delete any record in the tenant; (2) isAdmin=true with a mismatched tenantId — an admin may delete records in other tenants. RecordRef.ownerId is unused, so this is not an owner-or-admin check. The function is the public authorization contract; no in-repo caller is required for the bypass to be real.

findings.whyItBreaks: parseSettings is exported and used by updateFontSize. JSON.parse failures and the existing 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' throws are now caught and replaced with {theme:"light", fontSize:14}. Failure and a legitimate default config are indistinguishable. updateFontSize then always save()s that object with the new size, so invalid input that previously aborted the write now persists a fabricated theme (e.g. {"theme":"dark"} missing fontSize used to throw; now it saves theme "light").

findings.title: Do not swallow parseSettings failures as DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: parseSettings is exported and used by updateFontSize. Invalid JSON, a non-string theme, or a non-number fontSize previously threw, so save() never ran. The new empty catch maps every failure to {theme:"light", fontSize:14}. Callers cannot tell failure from a real default config. updateFontSize then always writes that object with the new size: e.g. updateFontSize('{"theme":"dark"}', 18, save) used to throw on missing fontSize and leave storage unchanged; it now persists {theme:"light", fontSize:18} and drops the dark theme.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported commit, not verified
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport still sets builtFrom to build.ref(branch) but now calls artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")). When those refs resolve to different commits, the returned report lists another ref's artifacts under the branch commit. Callers of this exported function receive a mismatched BuildReport with no other pairing signal.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the same commit as builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport still sets builtFrom from build.ref(branch) but now loads artifacts via build.ref("verified"). When those refs resolve to different commits, the report claims the branch commit while listing another commit's artifacts; the branch argument no longer selects the artifact set.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the branch commit, not a verified ref
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport still sets builtFrom to build.ref(branch) but now calls artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")). Those lookups use different ref names, so when the branch and verified refs resolve to different commits the returned report attributes another commit's artifacts to the branch commit. The public function still takes branch as the report subject, so callers of buildReport(build, branch) receive a mismatched BuildReport.

findings.title: Restore slice cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The JSDoc and `limit` parameter still promise at most `limit` entries, newest first, but the new body only special-cases `limit <= 0` and otherwise returns the entire reversed copy. `renderFeed` calls `recentEntries(all, 20)`, preallocates `new Array(20)`, then copies `page.length` items. When `all.length > 20`, `page` is longer than 20, the loop extends `out`, and the feed page is unbounded.

findings.title: Restore slice so recentEntries returns at most `limit` items
findings.whyItBreaks: JSDoc and the previous implementation cap the result at `limit`. After this change, limit<=0 still returns [], but any positive limit returns the entire reversed copy. renderFeed calls recentEntries(all, 20) and copies page.length into the page buffer, so a feed longer than 20 is emitted in full instead of a 20-item page.

findings.title: Restore the `limit` cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: recentEntries previously returned `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`, honoring the JSDoc contract “at most `limit` entries, newest first.” The rewrite still takes `limit` and still documents that cap, but after `if (limit <= 0) return []` it returns the entire reversed copy. `renderFeed` calls `recentEntries(all, 20)`, preallocates 20 slots, then copies `page.length` items; when `all.length > 20` the output array grows past 20 instead of showing the 20 newest entries.

findings.title: Pass filtered length to `# entry-count`
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now drops stale entries from data rows via `live`, but still calls `headerLines(opts, entries.length)`. `# entry-count` therefore counts stale entries that are not listed. Any consumer that trusts the header (or checks count against parsed rows) sees a lie: e.g. 2 entries with one stale yields `entry-count: 2` and a single path line.

findings.title: Pass live.length into headerLines after dropping stale rows
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now omits stale entries from TSV rows but still calls headerLines(opts, entries.length). `# entry-count` therefore counts stale entries that are not in the body. Before this change, count always equaled the number of data rows; after it, any input with at least one stale entry emits a header that overstates the listing (all-stale input yields a positive count and zero rows). That is the serialized public contract of exported renderManifest.

findings.title: Pass live.length into entry-count after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now emits only !e.stale rows but still calls headerLines(opts, entries.length). # entry-count therefore counts omitted stale entries. Example: two entries with one stale yields '# entry-count: 2' and a single path\tsize row. That header is the public contract of exported renderManifest; any reader that sizes, checksums, or loops from entry-count will treat a complete live-only body as truncated (or accept a short body as complete).

findings.title: Keep check() False for non-str stored_hash so guard still 401s
findings.whyItBreaks: hmac.compare_digest requires two same-type ASCII str or bytes values. token_hash() always returns a str hexdigest, so stored_hash=None (also bytes/int/non-ASCII) now raises TypeError. The previous `token_hash(presented_token) == stored_hash` returned False for those inputs. guard() at line 14 uses `if not check(...)` and has no handler for that exception, so a missing/invalid stored token no longer returns {"status": 401} and crashes before either the 401 or handler branch.

findings.title: Stop making execute() always throw
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is the repo's only exported API and is typed to return string. The body previously returned input.toUpperCase(); it now unconditionally throws Error("always fails"), so every caller gets an exception instead of a result and the core path is unusable.

findings.title: Stop throwing from execute(); restore uppercase result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute() is the module's only exported API. It previously returned input.toUpperCase(); the new body throws Error("always fails") on every call, so callers never receive a string and the core path is unusable.

findings.title: Don't reject viewers in isEligible; it blocks handle's read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible now returns false when req.role === "viewer". handle is the only reader and short-circuits that to "rejected". Substituting {status:"active", role:"viewer", attempts:0}: previously isEligible was true and handle returned "read-only" at line 25; now isEligible is false so handle returns "rejected" and line 25 is unreachable. Role already had its own post-eligibility branch; the new gate does not legitimately govern the read-only action.

findings.title: Remove viewer check from isEligible; it blocks read-only handle
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible is the only gate in handle() (line 24). The new `req.role === "viewer"` branch makes every viewer ineligible, so handle returns "rejected" and never reaches the existing `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only"` arm. Precondition substitution: status="active", role="viewer", attempts=0 previously passed isEligible (active + attempts < 5) and returned "read-only"; it now fails isEligible at line 18 and returns "rejected". Read-only is a distinct, independently valid action for an active viewer under MAX_ATTEMPTS; a viewer-exclusion predicate does not govern it.

findings.title: Remove viewer gate from isEligible; it blocks read-only handle
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() is the only reader of isEligible and still has a distinct allowed action for viewers: after the eligibility gate it returns "read-only". Substituting role="viewer" with status="active" and attempts<5: isEligible now takes `req.role === "viewer"` at line 18 and returns false, so handle line 24 returns "rejected". Before this change that request passed isEligible (status+attempt cap only) and returned "read-only" at line 25. The new role clause does not legitimately govern that action; it over-blocks a path that remains in the handler.

findings.title: Stop blocking unpaid draft saves via shared canProceed
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now requires payment === "paid". saveDraft and submitOrder both gate on it. An unpaid draft (state="draft", payment="missing") previously saved (state !== "ready" was true); it now returns "blocked". Saving a draft is independent of payment, and "missing" is a valid Order.payment. submitOrder is a distinct action that payment may govern; saveDraft is not.

findings.title: Do not require payment on shared canProceed used by saveDraft
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now returns true only when state!=="ready" AND payment==="paid". saveDraft gates on the same predicate, so an unpaid draft (state="draft", payment="missing") previously saved and now returns "blocked". Saving a draft does not legitimately require payment.

findings.title: Don't require paid payment for saveDraft via shared canProceed
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now returns order.state !== "ready" && order.payment === "paid". That shared predicate gates two distinct actions. submitOrder may legitimately require payment, but saveDraft does not: an unpaid draft (state="draft", payment="missing") previously passed (state !== "ready") and saved; after this change canProceed is false, so saveDraft returns "blocked". Saving a draft is independently approvable without payment.

findings.title: Publish snapshot files from stable instead of channel HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot still records commit=repo.headCommit(channel) and channel as given, but files are now repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). For any channel whose HEAD is not the stable HEAD, the snapshot lies: callers receive another ref’s tree labeled as this channel’s commit. That is a broken publish contract on the only publish path (exported; no in-repo callers to mask it).

findings.title: Attach snapshot files from stable instead of channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot still sets Snapshot.commit to repo.headCommit(channel) and Snapshot.channel to the requested channel, but files are now repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). For any channel other than "stable" (including DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main"), the published file list is not the tree of the advertised commit. Pre-change code used filesAt(head), so commit and files stayed coherent. This is the exported publish contract; there are no in-repo callers to mask it.

findings.title: Publish snapshot files from channel HEAD, not hardcoded stable
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot(repo, channel) still records commit=repo.headCommit(channel) and Snapshot.channel=channel, but files are now repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). For any channel other than "stable" (including DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main"), the returned file list does not belong to the reported commit. Callers that persist, deploy, or verify Snapshot.files against Snapshot.commit will publish the wrong tree. The extra headCommit("stable") also makes every publish depend on a ref this repo never defines (DEFAULT_CHANNEL is "main").

findings.title: Wire build() limit into the loop instead of hardcoded max_count
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature build(prefix, limit=10) promises to cap the returned list at limit. The body never reads limit; it always loops range(max_count) with max_count hardcoded to 10, so build('x', limit=3) still returns 10 items and build('x', limit=20) still returns 10. Default callers are unchanged; any explicit limit is silently ignored.

findings.title: Honor `limit` in `build`; it never caps output
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=10)` is a public signature that promises callers can cap how many `{prefix}-{i}` entries are returned. The body never reads `limit` and always loops `range(max_count)` with `max_count = 10`, so `build('x', 3)` and `build('x', 50)` both return 10 items. That is the result a caller receives, not an unused no-op kwarg.

findings.title: Wire build() limit into the item loop
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature build(prefix, limit=10) promises a caller-controlled cap on how many items are returned. The body never reads limit; it still sets max_count = 10 and iterates range(max_count), so build('x', limit=3) and build('x', limit=20) both return 10 items. Existing no-limit callers keep working, but the new parameter is a false contract on result length.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name parse_positive_int promises a positive integer, but the body is only int(value), so 0 and negatives are returned unchanged. charge() calls it with no further check and multiplies by 100, so charge(-1) returns -100 and total_cents can sum negative cent amounts. Callers will skip their own positivity checks because the helper name already claims that work.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name parse_positive_int promises a positive integer, but the body is still `return int(value)` and accepts 0 and negatives (e.g. int(-5) == -5). charge() at line 6 uses that result as already-validated input and returns n*100, so non-positive amounts become billed/persisted cents with no error.

findings.title: Honor parse_positive_int positivity or drop the name
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name parse_positive_int promises to accept only integers > 0. The body is still return int(value), so 0 and negatives succeed. charge (line 6) now delegates to that name and performs no own positivity check, so charge(-5) returns -500 and total_cents includes it as billed cents. Callers that trust the name will skip validation and persist/bill non-positive amounts.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy in apply_values
findings.whyItBreaks: apply_values previously copied the input (`result = df.copy()`) and wrote mapped values only on that copy, so the caller’s frame stayed unchanged. The new body does `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` and `return df`, so every matching cell is overwritten on the object the caller passed. Any caller that keeps using `df` after the call (diff, retry, further transforms, shared references) now sees the mapped values as original data.

findings.title: Restore copy so apply_values does not mutate caller frames
findings.whyItBreaks: apply_values previously copied the input DataFrame, wrote mapped values onto the copy, and returned that independent object, leaving the caller's frame unchanged. The new body assigns through df.loc[...] and returns df, so the argument object is mutated and aliased with the return value. Any caller that keeps using the original frame (compare-before/after, reuse, share across steps) now observes the mapped values as a silent side effect.

findings.title: Restore copy so apply_values does not mutate caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body copied the input (`result = df.copy()`) then assigned into the copy, so the caller's DataFrame stayed unchanged and the return value was a distinct object. The new body does `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` and `return df`, which mutates the input object in place (pandas `.loc` assignment writes through) and aliases the return value to that same object. Any caller that still holds `df` after the call now sees overwritten `value` cells; even an empty mapping changes identity (`apply_values(df, {}) is df` is now True).

findings.title: Make parse_positive_int reject non-positive values
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name parse_positive_int promises a parsed value n > 0. The body is still s.parse().unwrap_or(0), so negatives succeed ("-5" → -5) and invalid input becomes 0. charge trusts that result and returns n * 100, so charge("-5") is -500 and charge("abc") is 0 with no error.

findings.title: Honor positivity promised by parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public symbol was renamed to parse_positive_int, which promises the returned i64 is positive. The body is still s.parse().unwrap_or(0): negatives pass through, 0 is returned for both a parsed zero and any parse error, and nothing filters n > 0. charge() trusts that result and does n * 100 with no further check, so charge("-5") bills -500 and charge("abc") bills 0 as if a real amount.

findings.title: Implement positivity in parse_positive_int or revert the name
findings.whyItBreaks: The public rename to parse_positive_int promises a positive integer. The body is still s.parse().unwrap_or(0): "-5" returns -5, "0" returns 0, and "abc" also returns 0. charge (src/parse.rs:6-7) skips any positivity check and does n * 100, so charge("-5") is -500 and a parse failure is billed as a real zero amount.

findings.title: Avoid moving items in dbg! before calling len()
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg!(items) as a statement matches the Vec by value, prints it, and drops the returned tmp. items is then uninitialized, so items.len() is a use-after-move (E0382) and the public process path cannot compile.

findings.whyItBreaks: dbg!(items) evaluates items by value (std::dbg matches the expr, prints, and returns the temporary). The return is discarded, so items is moved. items.len() on the next line is then a use-after-move; the public process function does not compile and cannot return the count.

findings.whyItBreaks: std::dbg! takes its argument by value and returns it. `dbg!(items);` moves `items` (Vec<String> is not Copy) and discards the returned Vec, so `items.len()` is use-after-move (E0382) and the public `process` path does not compile.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against the same revision as fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset.fromRevision is documented as the revision changedPaths were computed against, and consumers replay those paths on exactly that revision. buildChangeset still sets fromRevision to store.resolve(pinnedTag) but now calls store.readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")). When pinnedTag is not "latest", the returned path list is the delta from a different revision than the apply base, so replay on fromRevision applies the wrong (typically incomplete) path set.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against latest, not fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset documents that fromRevision is the revision changedPaths were computed against and that consumers replay those paths on exactly that revision. Store.readChangedPaths(fromRevision) is the matching computation. After this change, fromRevision is still store.resolve(pinnedTag) but changedPaths is store.readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")). When pinnedTag is not latest, the path set is not the delta for the returned base: if readChangedPaths means "since this revision", latest typically yields an empty/near-empty list and replay on the pin skips real changes; if it means a snapshot at that revision, latest's paths are applied onto the pinned revision. Either way the public replay contract is wrong.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against fromRevision, not latest
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset promises fromRevision is the revision changedPaths were computed against, and that consumers replay onto exactly that revision. The body still sets fromRevision to store.resolve(pinnedTag) but now fills changedPaths via store.readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")). When pinnedTag is not latest, those lists diverge: replay on the pin applies a latest-based path set (missing pin→latest changes, or applying latest-relative paths onto the pin).
