findings.title: Propagate Gateway.Submit errors from Charge
findings.whyItBreaks: On gw.Submit error, Charge previously returned fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err). It now log.Printf's the error and falls through to return nil. Charge is an exported payment API whose error result is the only success/failure signal; callers that treat err == nil as 'charged' will record, fulfill, or skip retry for a payment that never succeeded. Logging does not make failure distinguishable at the API boundary.

findings.title: Propagate Submit errors instead of returning nil
findings.whyItBreaks: Charge still advertises `error`, but on gw.Submit failure it only log.Printf's the error and then falls through to `return nil`. Callers that key off `err != nil` cannot distinguish a failed charge from success and will proceed as if payment went through (fulfill, mark paid, skip retry). Invalid-amount still returns an error, so the contract is inconsistent: validation failures surface, processor failures look like success. This is an exported public swallow (TRIGGER D); there are no in-repo callers, but every future caller is forced to conflate failure with a real nil.

findings.title: Return gateway Submit errors from Charge instead of nil
findings.whyItBreaks: Charge is an exported error-returning API. On gw.Submit failure it previously returned a wrapped error so callers could abort fulfillment; it now log.Printf's the error and falls through to return nil. Callers that treat a nil error as a successful charge will persist, fulfill, or bill as if payment succeeded. Invalid amounts still error (lines 13–14), so only the live gateway-failure path is silently converted into success.

findings.title: Include tenantId in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) is `settings:${name}` while settingsFor still fetches store.fetch(tenantId, name). The module-level Map is therefore shared across tenants: after tenant A caches setting N, tenant B's settingsFor(B, N) hits that entry at line 13-14 and returns A's value without calling fetch. cache.set at line 16 also overwrites the shared slot, so later reads for A can see B. invalidate(name) matches this unscoped key and cannot target one tenant. Tenant isolation that the previous `${tenantId}:${name}` key enforced is gone.

findings.title: Keep tenantId in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still takes tenantId and still calls store.fetch(tenantId, name) on miss, but cache identity is now only `settings:${name}`. After tenant A caches setting `theme`, tenant B's settingsFor(B, 'theme') takes the hit !== undefined branch and returns A's value without fetching. The shared slot is also last-writer-wins, so A can later observe B's value. That is cross-tenant disclosure of tenant-scoped settings.

findings.title: Keep tenantId in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still takes tenantId and store.fetch(tenantId, name) is tenant-scoped, but cacheKey is only `settings:${name}`. After tenant A populates the Map, tenant B’s settingsFor(B, name) takes the cache-hit branch (hit !== undefined) and returns A’s value without calling fetch. That is a cross-tenant disclosure. invalidate(name) is the matching public-API break: old invalidate(tenantId, name) callers either fail typecheck or, at runtime, delete `settings:${tenantId}` and leave `settings:${name}` in place.

findings.title: Serialize reserve check/decrement around store.save
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve reads remaining, then awaits this.store.save(sku, remaining - 1) before this.stock.set. The await yields, so a second reserve(sku) can run, observe the same remaining > 0, also save remaining-1, and also return true. Two callers can therefore reserve the last unit (e.g. load(sku, 1) then Promise.all of two reserve() calls both succeed), and both writes persist the same snapshot remaining-1 (last write wins) instead of decrementing twice. The pre-change body was synchronous, so the check-and-set could not interleave on the event loop.

findings.title: Don't await store.save between stock check and decrement
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve reads remaining, then awaits this.store.save before this.stock.set. await always yields a microtask, even if save resolves immediately, so a second reserve on the same SKU can run while the first is in flight and still see the old count. Both pass remaining <= 0, both persist remaining-1, both return true. With stock=1, two concurrent reserve(sku) calls both succeed and the store records 0 instead of rejecting the second claim.

findings.title: Claim stock before awaiting save to prevent oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads remaining and checks remaining <= 0, then awaits store.save before this.stock.set. In JavaScript that await yields, so a second reserve() on the same SKU can run while the first is still in flight. Both calls observe the same remaining, both pass the guard, both persist remaining - 1, and both return true. With remaining === 1 that sells two units of one item and writes 0 once instead of failing the second call. The same lost update happens for remaining > 1: two concurrent reserves persist the same remaining - 1, so the store and the in-memory map drop only one unit for two successful reservations. Sequential callers were race-free before this await existed.

findings.title: Stop treating millisecond backoff as seconds in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed from a seconds delay capped at 30 to milliseconds capped at 30_000. schedulePoll was updated to pass that value straight to setTimeout, but retry still does sleep(backoff(a) * 1000) into a millisecond setTimeout. Substitution: backoff(0)=1000 → sleep(1_000_000) so the first retry waits ~16.7 minutes instead of 1s; at the cap, backoff(a)=30_000 → sleep(30_000_000) so later retries wait 8.3 hours instead of 30s. Job retries hang instead of backing off.

findings.title: Update retry sleep to match millisecond backoff units
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() previously returned seconds (capped at 30) and both callers converted to ms via * 1000. This change makes backoff return milliseconds (capped at 30_000) and updates schedulePoll, but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). sleep() already treats its argument as ms, so attempt 0 waits 1_000_000 ms (≈16.7 min) instead of 1000 ms, and the cap waits 30_000_000 ms (≈8.3 h) instead of 30 s. Job retries stall rather than back off.

findings.title: Stop scaling retry delays after converting backoff to milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff used to return seconds capped at 30 (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)). Both callers converted to ms with * 1000. This PR returns ms directly (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)) and updates schedulePoll, but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000) where sleep already takes milliseconds. Substitution: attempt 0 is 1000ms, then * 1000 → 1_000_000ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1s; at the cap, 30_000 * 1000 → 30_000_000ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30s. Job retries stall by 1000x.

findings.title: Propagate File.Close error after a successful flush
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Save ended with `return f.Close()`, so a close failure after buffered writes was visible to callers. Head always `defer f.Close()` (error discarded) and `return w.Flush()`. Flush only pushes the bufio buffer into *os.File; Close can still fail (NFS delayed write, ENOSPC, interrupt). On that path Save now returns nil, so callers treat a failed persist as success. Save is exported; there are no in-repo callers, but the public error contract itself now conflates close failure with success.

findings.title: Propagate file Close errors instead of discarding them in defer
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous success path was `return f.Close()`, so a Close failure after a successful Flush (late ENOSPC, NFS, interrupted close) was returned to the caller. `defer f.Close()` now drops that error, and `return w.Flush()` reports nil whenever the buffer is written. Exported `Save` therefore conflates “flushed to the kernel” with “file closed successfully”; callers cannot distinguish a failed persist from a real save.

findings.title: Propagate os.File.Close error from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Save returned f.Close() after a successful Flush, so delayed write/close failures reached the caller as a non-nil error. Head defers f.Close() (error discarded) and returns only w.Flush(). Save is exported; a nil error now means only that the bufio buffer flushed, not that the file closed successfully. Callers cannot distinguish a completed save from a close failure and may skip retry or treat missing data as written.

findings.title: Stop dropping the last row of each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds documents and returns a half-open [start, end) interval (end = min(start + page_size, row_count)), matching the pre-change loop range(start, end). The new loop range(start, end - 1) never yields index end-1, so page_window omits the last row of every non-empty page. Downstream render_page/_format_row only number the truncated window, and summarize therefore emits every page minus its last row. Concrete substitution: rows=['a','b','c','d'], page_index=0, page_size=2 → start=0, end=2 → range(0, 1) → ['a'] (missing 'b'). With page_size=1, start=k, end=k+1 → range(k, k) is empty, so every page is [] and summarize is only blank sections joined by ---.

findings.title: Do not drop the last item of each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: Base page_window used range(start, end) over half-open bounds. Head still computes those same bounds in _window_bounds (end = min(start + page_size, row_count)), but the loop is now range(start, end - 1), so index end-1 is never collected. Every page loses its last row; they are not shifted to the next page because the next page still starts at page_index * page_size. Concrete substitution: rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=2 → page 0 bounds [0,2) yields only ['a']; page 1 [2,4) yields only ['c']; page 2 [4,5) yields range(4,4)=[] so 'e' disappears. With page_size=1, every page is empty. render_page (L40) and summarize (L51-52) therefore omit those rows and can emit blank pages.

findings.title: Stop dropping the last row of every page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds documents and returns a half-open [start, end) interval (end = min(start + page_size, row_count)). page_window then iterates range(start, end - 1), so index end-1 is never included. Concrete substitution: rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=2, page_index=0 → start=0,end=2 → range(0,1) yields ['a'] instead of ['a','b']; page_index=2 → start=4,end=5 → range(4,4) yields [] instead of ['e']. page_size=1 makes every page empty. render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) inherit the omitted rows.

findings.title: Restore age < ttl hit test in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshness predicate flipped from `Date.now() - storedAt < ttlMs` (hit) to `> ttlMs`. A get with age 0 (immediately after set, ttlMs > 0) takes the else branch, deletes the entry, and returns null. Once age exceeds ttlMs the expired value is returned. The cache is inverted: misses while fresh, hits after expiry.

findings.title: Stop splicing jobs while forEach is iterating
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach walks a live index while `splice(index, 1)` shifts later elements left, so the item that moves into the current index is never visited. Input `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]`: index 0 splices the first done job, the second done job shifts to index 0, forEach continues at index 1 (the pending job). Result is `[{done:true},{done:false}]` — a done job remains. Unlike `filter`, this also mutates the caller’s array in place.

findings.title: Restore TTL less-than check so unexpired entries are returned
findings.whyItBreaks: get() now returns a value only when age > ttlMs and otherwise deletes the entry and returns null. A still-valid entry (age < ttlMs) is evicted as a miss; an expired entry is returned as a hit. Equality (age == ttlMs) still expires under both operators, so only the interiors of the live and expired ranges are swapped. TtlCache.get's public TTL contract is inverted.

findings.title: Stop splicing inside forEach; consecutive done jobs are skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#forEach snapshots length and always increments the index. splice(index, 1) shifts the next job into the current slot, which is never visited. For [done, done, active], the second done job remains. The previous filter(!job.done) removed every done job and did not mutate the input; this also mutates the caller's array in place.

findings.title: Restore TTL check; live entries miss and stale ones are served
findings.whyItBreaks: TtlCache.get used to treat age < ttlMs as a hit. The flipped `>` now returns a value only after expiry and, in the else branch, deletes the entry and returns null. Substitution: after set(), age≈0; for any ttlMs>0, `0 > ttlMs` is false, so a just-written key is evicted and get() returns null. Once age exceeds ttlMs, the expired value is returned as if still live.

findings.title: Stop splicing during forEach; consecutive done jobs survive prune
findings.whyItBreaks: filter() removed every job with done===true and returned a new array. forEach captures the original length, then splice(index,1) shifts later elements left so the next done job occupies an already-consumed index and is never visited. Substitution: [done, done, open] → visit 0, splice → [done, open], visit 1 (open), visit 2 (hole) → result [done, open]. Adjacent done jobs are left behind. The input array is also mutated in place, unlike the previous non-mutating contract.

findings.title: Restore empty-array guard so averageAmount does not return NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-length guard that returned 0 was removed. For rows=[], reduce yields 0 and 0/rows.length is 0/0, which is NaN. That value is a number in TypeScript but fails Number.isFinite and poisons any later arithmetic, equality, or aggregation that previously received 0.

findings.title: Copy rows before sorting in busiest to avoid mutating callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates in place. The previous `[...rows]` copy was dropped, so `busiest(rows)` reorders the caller’s array by descending amount. Callers that still use `rows` after the call (display order, later reductions, identity with a stored snapshot) now observe a different sequence even though the function’s documented result is only the top Row or null.

findings.title: Restore empty-array guard in averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-length early return was removed. reduce still yields 0, then `0 / rows.length` is `0 / 0`, which is NaN in JS. Callers that previously received 0 now get NaN, which poisons arithmetic, comparisons, and JSON serialization.

findings.title: Copy before sorting in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort` reorders its receiver in place. Dropping `[...rows]` means `busiest(rows)` mutates the caller’s array order as a side effect of picking the max-amount row.

findings.title: Keep averageAmount([]) returning 0, not NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array guard was removed. [].reduce(..., 0) is 0, then 0 / 0 is NaN. Callers that previously got 0 now get a poisonous non-number (toFixed throws, === comparisons fail, JSON.stringify emits null).

findings.title: Stop busiest() from sorting the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates and returns the same array. Dropping `[...rows]` reorders the caller's rows descending by amount, so later reads of that array see a different sequence than the one they passed in.

findings.title: Rank scores numerically; default sort is lexicographic
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no compareFn stringifies elements and orders UTF-16 code units, then reverse() flips that — it is not numeric descending. Previously scores.sort((a, b) => b - a) produced a true nth-highest cutoff. Substitution: players [{a:9},{b:80},{c:70}], n=2 → rankScores string-sorts [9,80,70] to [70,80,9], reverse → [9,80,70], cutoff = scores[1] = 80, filter p.score >= 80 keeps only 80 (slice(0,2) still [b]). Correct numeric desc is [80,70,9], cutoff 70, result [b,c]. Same miss on any mixed-digit set (9 vs 10, 99 vs 100, negatives).

findings.title: Use a numeric comparator in rankScores sort
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparefn stringifies numbers and orders them lexicographically, then reverse() yields string-descending order. topPlayers takes cutoff from that array, so mixed-magnitude scores rank incorrectly. Example: scores [9, 10, 11], n=2 → string-desc [9, 11, 10], cutoff=11, filter keeps only 11. Previous numeric sort((a,b)=>b-a) gave [11, 10, 9], cutoff=10, and returned 11 and 10.

findings.title: Use numeric descending sort in rankScores
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no compareFn orders by UTF-16 string order, not numeric value. The previous comparator was (a, b) => b - a. After this change, [9, 10] becomes [9, 10] ("10" < "9", then reverse), so n=1 cutoff is 9 and topPlayers/formatBoard can return the score-9 player instead of 10. Asking for top 3 of [9, 80, 100] sets cutoff to 100 and drops two players who should be included.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the auth gate for handle(): a True result runs processor(payload); False returns 401. The old body used hmac.compare_digest, which does not short-circuit. The new body uses str ==, which in CPython returns on the first mismatched hex nibble of the SHA-256 hexdigest. An attacker who can measure verify/handle latency can recover the expected signature prefix-by-prefix and then forge webhooks. Functional accept/reject for same-type strings is unchanged; the security property of the comparison is not.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the webhook auth gate (handle returns 401 vs invoking processor). The old body used hmac.compare_digest, which is constant-time. CPython str == returns at the first mismatched character of the SHA-256 hex digest, so an attacker who controls given_signature can recover expected MAC bytes from response timing and then forge payloads that pass verify and execute processor(). Auth success/failure for honest same-type inputs is unchanged; the comparison primitive is the defect.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC compare in webhook verify
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the only auth gate for handle(). Replacing hmac.compare_digest with str == lets Python short-circuit on the first differing hex character, leaking the expected HMAC via response timing so an attacker can iteratively forge a valid given_signature and reach processor(payload).

findings.title: Apply balances inside the same transaction as the ledger insert
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the ledger INSERT and both account UPDATEs ran inside `with db.transaction()`, so they committed or rolled back together. The refactor commits `_record_ledger` on context exit, then calls `_apply_balances` outside that block. A crash or exception after the `with` (or between the debit and credit UPDATEs, which now have no wrapping transaction) leaves a committed ledger row without matching balances, or a debit without a credit. Callers that treat the raised error as a failed transfer and retry will insert a second ledger row and can apply the amount twice.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Base `transfer` ran the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs inside one `with db.transaction():` block. Head commits `_record_ledger` on context exit, then calls `_apply_balances` (two UPDATEs) with no wrapping transaction. If either UPDATE fails or the process dies after the `with` block, the ledger records a transfer that did not move money; if the debit succeeds and the credit fails, `from_acct` loses cents that never reach `to_acct`. The caller still sees the exception, but persisted state is already split.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code ran the ledger INSERT and both account UPDATEs in one `with db.transaction():` block. The refactor still commits `_record_ledger` on successful `__exit__`, then calls `_apply_balances` after that commit. If either UPDATE fails, the process crashes between the two phases, or the credit UPDATE fails after the debit, the ledger (and possibly the source debit) is already durable while the destination credit is not — funds and the audit trail diverge.

findings.title: Keep billingDay on UTC, not host local time
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay previously keyed the day from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a given instant always produced the same YYYY-MM-DD. It now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which are the runtime's local zone. sameBillingDay compares those strings, so two instants on the same UTC day that straddle local midnight no longer match, and any persisted UTC day key will miss after upgrade. Example: 2026-01-01T05:00:00.000Z is 2026-01-01 in UTC but 2025-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles; pairing it with 2026-01-01T12:00:00.000Z used to be sameBillingDay true and is now false whenever TZ is west of UTC.

findings.title: Restore UTC calendar fields in billingDay
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay previously formatted the UTC calendar date (getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate). It now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which follow the host timezone. For any instant in the local UTC-offset window (e.g. 2026-01-01T00:30:00.000Z in America/Los_Angeles), the returned key changes from 2026-01-01 to 2025-12-31. sameBillingDay therefore treats two timestamps on the same UTC day that straddle local midnight as different days (and the reverse). Results also differ across machines/CI vs production TZ, so any stored billing-day key from the old UTC contract will not match.

findings.title: Keep billingDay on the UTC calendar, not local time
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously billingDay used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a given instant always mapped to one YYYY-MM-DD key. It now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which are host-local. For new Date('2026-01-01T00:30:00.000Z') on America/Los_Angeles that returns '2025-12-31' instead of '2026-01-01'. sameBillingDay inherits this: new Date('2026-01-01T00:30:00.000Z') and new Date('2026-01-01T12:00:00.000Z') are the same UTC billing day but compare false in UTC-8 because they fall on different local dates. Billing keys therefore differ by deploy TZ and break any stored UTC day strings.

findings.title: Restore tenant in the profile memo key
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile still takes tenant and fetchProfile(tenant, account), and Profile includes tenant, but the module-level memo is now keyed only by account. After readProfile("t1", "acct") stores under "acct", readProfile("t2", "acct") hits that entry at memo.get and returns t1's Profile without calling fetchProfile. A later fetch for t2 also memo.set-overwrites the same slot, so t1 then receives t2's Profile.

findings.title: Restore tenant in the profile memo key
findings.whyItBreaks: memo is a process-wide Map. After this change the lookup key is only `account`, while fetch still loads by (tenant, account) and Profile still carries tenant. Once tenant A caches account X, tenant B requesting the same account hits `if (cached) return cached` and receives A's Profile (A's tenant and displayName) instead of calling fetchProfile('B', X). That is cross-tenant data leak and a wrong result on the public API.

findings.title: Include tenant in the profile memo key
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile is exported as a tenant+account lookup (fetchProfile still takes both; Profile includes tenant). The process-wide Map is now keyed only by account. After readProfile('t1','alice', fetch) caches t1's profile, readProfile('t2','alice', fetch) hits memo.get('alice') and returns t1's Profile without calling fetchProfile — cross-tenant data disclosure and a wrong identity. A later miss for t2 also memo.set('alice', t2Profile) and poisons t1's subsequent reads.

findings.title: Do not swallow missing-key errors as empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: load() previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when store.get returned undefined. The new empty catch returns "", which is also a legitimate Map value. Exported load() and in-repo loadAll() can no longer distinguish a missing key from a present empty string; loadAll previously aborted on the first miss and now silently fills holes with "". Any exception from store.get is discarded the same way.

findings.title: Stop swallowing missing-key errors as empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: load() previously threw on a missing key. The new catch-all returns "". Map<string,string> may legitimately store "", so callers cannot tell failure from a real value. loadAll maps through load, so a missing key no longer fails the batch and is persisted/returned as an empty slot. The empty catch also hides non-missing errors (e.g. a non-Map store). This is an exported contract change: every caller is forced to conflate failure with a stored empty string.

findings.title: Stop mapping missing-key errors to empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: load() previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when store.get returned undefined. The new catch-all returns "", which is also a legal Map<string,string> value, so callers cannot tell failure from a present empty string. loadAll maps through load and therefore now returns an array with "" slots instead of aborting on the first missing key.

findings.title: Propagate retryBackground failures instead of returning void
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a new public export. fn() exceptions are caught with an empty handler and continued; timeout (line 23) and retry exhaustion (end of the loop) also return void. Callers cannot distinguish success from failure, timeout, or exhaustion, so a failed run is observed as a normal return. There is no log and no error channel. As an exported swallow site this is a broken contract even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Rethrow the last error when retryBackground gives up
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a new exported function. On each failed attempt the empty catch discards the exception; on deadline expiry line 23 returns; after the loop it falls through. Success also returns void (line 26). Callers are forced to treat a failed or timed-out run as the same undefined result as success, and nothing logs the error either.

findings.title: Rethrow after retryBackground exhausts retries or times out
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is an exported void API. On success it returns at line 26. On timeout it returns at line 23. On each thrown attempt the empty catch at lines 27-29 discards the error; after the loop it falls off line 31. Callers therefore receive the same undefined/non-throwing completion for success, timeout, and exhausted retries, and will treat failed work as done.

findings.title: Do not read .length on string | number Field value
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now string | number, so callers may pass a number. Numbers have no length, so value.length is undefined at runtime and the input's defaultValue becomes 'len=undefined' instead of a digit count. TypeScript also cannot resolve .length on string | number.

findings.title: Do not read .length on string|number value
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now string | number, but the body interpolates value.length. Primitive numbers have no length, so a numeric value (including 0) yields defaultValue "len=undefined" instead of a digit count. This is an exported public contract: callers may pass a number and observe a wrong result.

findings.title: Coerce Field value before reading .length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now string | number, but the body uses value.length. Numbers have no length, so a numeric value yields undefined and the input's defaultValue becomes the string "len=undefined" instead of a length. The exported union also fails type-checking (Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number').

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN in the deploy workflow
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step copies secrets.TOKEN into env TOKEN and runs echo "deploying with $TOKEN". That writes the deploy credential to the Actions step log (stdout). GitHub redaction is best-effort and incomplete (values shorter than 4 characters, some encodings/whitespace, debug/set -x traces); GitHub's own guidance is to treat any printed secret as compromised and rotate it. Anyone who can read workflow logs (public repo: everyone; private: anyone with repo read) can recover an unmasked value. The env block is also step-scoped, so TOKEN never reaches `make build` — the only effect of this hunk is exposing the secret.

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN into GitHub Actions logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step assigns secrets.TOKEN to env TOKEN and runs echo "deploying with $TOKEN" on ubuntu-latest (bash). That writes the credential to the step's stdout, which is the Actions job log. Log redaction is best-effort (fails for short values, encoded/split forms, and some runner/debug drains) and is not a security boundary; anyone who can read workflow logs can recover a deploy token. The value is not passed to make build, so the step has no purpose other than printing the secret.

findings.title: Do not echo secrets.TOKEN into GitHub Actions logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step copies secrets.TOKEN into the shell environment and runs echo "deploying with $TOKEN". That writes the deploy credential to job stdout, which GitHub Actions persists as the workflow log on every push. Masking is best-effort only (short or empty values, debug logging, and several known bypasses are not redacted) and is not a confidentiality control; anyone who can read Actions logs can recover the token, which defeats the secrets store. The env is also scoped to this echo step, so the leak is not even required for make build.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer on git spawnSync
findings.whyItBreaks: Node spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1MiB. git() is what captures the full PR patch (`git diff mergeBase headSha` at line 140). When that stdout exceeds 1MiB, Node kills git (status=null, signal=SIGTERM, error ENOBUFS). git() treats null status as failure and throws, so runGithub posts a failure check and never reviews. That is a regression from the previous 64MiB cap, which gh()/ghText() still use.

findings.title: Set bundle.baseSha to mergeBase, not PR_BASE_SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha is PR_BASE_SHA or merge-base(origin/main, HEAD). mergeBase is merge-base(baseSha, headSha). patch and changedFiles still use mergeBase, but the bundle now passes the shorthand `baseSha`. When PR_BASE_SHA is the GitHub base-branch tip (the usual value of that env var), it is not the PR merge-base, so bundle.baseSha is not the left side of bundle.patch. review(bundle) then gets a SHA range that disagrees with the provided patch and file list.

findings.title: Pass merge-base as bundle.baseSha so it matches patch and files
findings.whyItBreaks: patch and changedFiles are still computed from mergeBase (git merge-base of PR_BASE_SHA/origin-main and headSha). The bundle now stores baseSha, which is process.env.PR_BASE_SHA or merge-base(origin/main, HEAD). GitHub Actions PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip, not the fork point. Whenever that tip has moved past the PR's merge-base, bundle.baseSha no longer names the left-hand commit of patch/changedFiles. review(bundle) then sees a SHA that does not correspond to the supplied diff (file contents and line mapping at the tip diverge from the patch).

findings.title: Restore 64MB maxBuffer on git spawnSync for large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is the path that loads the full PR patch via `git diff mergeBase headSha`. spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1MiB (1024*1024). The previous 64MiB cap (still used by gh/ghText) is gone, so any patch over ~1MB kills the child (status null, ENOBUFS). runGithub then posts a failed check instead of reviewing. Moderate PRs with lockfiles or generated files routinely exceed 1MB of unified diff.

findings.title: Restore git spawnSync maxBuffer of 64MiB
findings.whyItBreaks: git() captures the full PR patch via spawnSync('git', ['diff', mergeBase, headSha]). Omitting maxBuffer uses Node’s default of 1024*1024 bytes (child_process MAX_BUFFER). Output above 1MiB kills the child (status null, ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER); git() then throws on res.status !== 0. runGithub’s catch posts a failed check-run and sets process.exitCode = 1, so any PR whose unified diff exceeds 1MiB (lockfiles, modest multi-file changes) fails closed. The previous 64MiB cap is still used by gh()/ghText, so this is a reduction, not unlimited buffering.

findings.title: Restore -s read-only on non-interactive Codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and no approval loop (`exec` does not prompt). The previous argv pinned `-s read-only`, which is the highest-precedence Codex sandbox override and is the documented CI/review posture. After this change the sandbox is taken from project `.codex/config.toml` (trusted trees), `~/.codex/config.toml`, or a looser default. Typical `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` (or `danger-full-access`) then lets the model edit the target repo and run mutating commands with no human gate. That is a sandbox bypass of a control this function previously enforced; for a review runner operating on untrusted trees it is also an injection/write surface.

findings.title: Restore -s read-only on Codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex previously forced `codex exec -s read-only`, which overrides $CODEX_HOME/config.toml. The new argv omits `-s`, so sandbox_mode comes from user/project config (or whatever the installed CLI default is). spawnSync still uses cwd=opts.repoPath with the caller prompt on stdin. On any host where sandbox_mode is workspace-write or danger-full-access (typical interactive Codex setup), the agent can now edit or run commands in the target repo. Official exec default is still read-only, but that default only applies when no config override is present; the CLI flag was the pin that made this wrapper always read-only.

findings.title: Keep `-s read-only` on non-interactive codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` still spawns `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and no `--ignore-user-config`. `codex exec` never prompts for approval, so `-s/--sandbox` is the only explicit privilege pin. Removing `"-s", "read-only"` lets Codex resolve sandbox from config (CLI flags beat project `.codex/config.toml` and `~/.codex/config.toml`, which commonly set `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or `danger-full-access`). On those hosts the agent can mutate `repoPath` and run shell commands that the previous invocation blocked. Built-in exec default being read-only does not restore the pin once user/project config is in the precedence chain.

findings.title: Restore merge-base between base and head for PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous range was git diff $(merge-base baseSha headSha) headSha (PR-only, three-dot). This now runs git diff baseSha HEAD. PR_BASE_SHA is the live base-branch tip and is often not an ancestor of the PR head; two-dot then folds in the reverse of every commit that landed on main after the branch point (and can hide PR files that already match current main). The same SHA is passed into changedFileSet, which already does git diff --name-only <sha> HEAD, so changedPaths, inline comments, and review(bundle) all see that wrong set. Switching the patch right-hand side from headSha (PR_HEAD_SHA) to HEAD also desyncs the patch from commit_id in postReview when checkout is not the PR tip.

findings.title: Restore merge-base for the GitHub PR patch and file set
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub still treats PR_BASE_SHA as the GitHub base-branch tip (fallback is already merge-base(origin/main, HEAD); env is not) and PR_HEAD_SHA as the review commit_id. The old range was git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) then git diff mergeBase headSha (GitHub three-dot / Files changed). The new range is git diff baseSha HEAD (two-dot trees) and changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) → git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD. When the workspace is the PR head and main has moved, that two-dot patch includes reverse diffs of base-only commits and omits the three-dot-only set; classifyFiles / bundle.patch / changedPaths therefore describe the wrong PR, and inlineComments can attach to paths GitHub’s review API will 422 (postReview then drops comments). When checkout is the Actions merge commit and PR_HEAD_SHA is the PR tip, the patch is taken against HEAD but postReview still sends commit_id: headSha, so comment line numbers need not exist on that commit.

findings.title: Restore merge-base + PR_HEAD_SHA for the GitHub PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub still reads PR_BASE_SHA (GitHub pull_request.base.sha is the base-branch tip, not the fork point) and PR_HEAD_SHA, then used to review git diff $(merge-base base head) headSha. The new git diff baseSha HEAD is a two-dot tree diff. When the PR is behind main, that patch includes the reverse of main's post-fork commits as if they were PR changes; review(bundle) therefore flags/misses the wrong hunks. changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) widens changedPaths the same way. Extra paths are not in GitHub's three-dot PR file list, so the reviews POST with inline comments 422s and the existing catch posts a body-only review — all inline comments drop. Independently, the patch right-hand side is now literal HEAD while postReview still sends commit_id: headSha; when PR_HEAD_SHA is set and the Actions checkout is the merge commit (default pull_request checkout), line comments are computed on a different tree than the commit they are attached to.

findings.title: Keep function replacers so patch `$` sequences stay literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement as a template: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched placeholder, `$``/`$'`→prompt text before/after the match. The previous `() => value` replacers insert text verbatim. `bundle.patch` is a raw git diff (shell `$'…'`, Make/`$$`, sed/perl/js `$&` are common), and `JSON.stringify` of the bundle/findings preserves those `$` sequences. After this change, `runCodex` is given a mutated review or critic prompt, so the model reviews different content than the PR.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so $ in patches is not interpolated
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement runs GetSubstitution: $$ → $, $& → the matched placeholder ({{BUNDLE}}/{{FINDINGS}}/{{PATCH}}), $` → template text before the match, $' → template text after it. bundle.patch is a raw git diff; JSON.stringify also leaves $ unescaped. A patch containing $' injects the rest of critic.md into the payload; $& is replaced by the placeholder token; $$ drops a dollar. runCodex then reviews corrupted content. The previous () => value replacers insert the string literally.

findings.title: Keep function replacers; string replace corrupts $ sequences
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement runs GetSubstitution. The previous `() => ...` replacers inserted the payload literally; the new string arguments rewrite `$$` → `$`, `$&` → the matched placeholder (`{{BUNDLE}}` / `{{FINDINGS}}` / `{{PATCH}}`), `$`` → the prompt prefix, and `$'` → the prompt suffix. `bundle.patch` and `JSON.stringify(bundle)` routinely contain those sequences (shell `$$`, JS/regex `$&`, etc.), so `runCodex` is given a mutated review/critic prompt: dollars dropped, placeholders reinserted into the payload, or the rest of the template duplicated into the patch. Node confirms: `JSON.stringify({patch:"foo $$ bar $& baz"})` becomes `{"patch":"foo $ bar {{BUNDLE}} baz"}`.

findings.title: Stop coercing malformed findings into real P1 defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding used to throw on non-object input and on missing/invalid severity, category, file, title, whyItBreaks, suggestedFix, lineStart, and lineEnd. Those throws were the only failure signal. The new body never throws on a partial object: invalid/missing severity becomes "P1", invalid category becomes "bug", missing title becomes "Untitled finding", missing file/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix become "", and lineStart/lineEnd become Number(...) with no isFinite/>0 check (missing → 0, non-numeric → NaN). normalizeReview dropped the strict flag (default true) and always maps through this function, so a payload like findings:[{}] is now a published P1/bug finding instead of a malformed-review error. The functions are exported; every caller is forced to treat failure as a real finding.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating P1 defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding used to throw on non-object input, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-finite or non-positive lineStart/lineEnd. Those Errors previously escaped through normalizeReview's default strict path (raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)). The new body never throws on field validation: invalid/missing severity becomes P1, invalid category becomes bug, missing title becomes "Untitled finding", missing file/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix become "", and lineStart/lineEnd become 0 or NaN (Number("x") is NaN; JSON.stringify then emits null). Callers can no longer tell a parse failure from a legitimate P1 finding. normalizeReview(raw, false) previously dropped invalid items; the strict flag is gone, so garbage is now kept as fabricated findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of defaulting them to P1
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding used to throw on a non-object, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or non-positive/non-finite line range. It now always returns a Finding, substituting severity "P1", category "bug", title "Untitled finding", file "", lineStart/lineEnd 0, and empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix. Those are legitimate field values, so callers cannot tell a parse failure from a real P1 bug. normalizeReview dropped both the default-strict throw and the strict=false drop-on-error path and always maps through that coercion, so a review with an empty/partial finding object is accepted and the synthetic record is returned in RawReview.findings. Invalid lineStart such as "abc" also becomes NaN (Number.isFinite was removed).

findings.title: Do not drop -R from gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the only SHA source for workflow_dispatch (EVENT_HEAD is empty because there is no pull_request payload). This step runs before actions/checkout. `gh pr view <number>` without `-R`/`GH_REPO` resolves the repo from git remotes and does not read `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`. A clean workspace has no remotes, so the command fails and Checkout PR head never gets a head OID. On this self-hosted runner a leftover clone can make `gh` query a different repo's PR with the same number and check out the wrong SHAs.

findings.title: Restore -R for gh pr view; it runs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the live workflow_dispatch path: EVENT_HEAD is empty because github.event.pull_request.head.sha is unset, so this step must call gh pr view before actions/checkout. gh resolves the repo only from -R, GH_REPO, or local git remotes (OverrideBaseRepoFunc reads GH_REPO only; cli/cli#3556 for GITHUB_REPOSITORY is unimplemented). GitHub Actions sets GITHUB_REPOSITORY, not GH_REPO, and GITHUB_WORKSPACE has no clone yet. Result: gh errors (not a git repository / no remotes) and the job never gets PR SHAs, or on a self-hosted runner with a leftover clone it may view PR $PR_NUM in a different repo. Checkout then uses steps.refs.outputs.head, so manual review is broken or reviews the wrong refs.

findings.title: Restore -R for pre-checkout gh pr view
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch runs on workflow_dispatch, when EVENT_HEAD is empty because github.event.pull_request is absent. That is the job's first step, before actions/checkout. gh resolves the repository from -R/--repo, then GH_REPO, then local git remotes; it does not read GITHUB_REPOSITORY (cli/cli OverrideBaseRepoFunc). After this change none of those are set, so gh pr view fails with a not-a-git-repository / unable-to-determine-base-repository error and the step dies under Actions' bash -e, or on this self-hosted runner it may query leftover remotes from a prior job and check out the wrong SHAs.

findings.title: Do not parse candidate findings with strict=false
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict=true) maps every finding through normalizeFinding and throws on a malformed required field. Passing false selects the lenient branch, which catch-filters those errors to null and omits the finding. The only gate after that call is !candidate.summary || candidate.checked.length === 0 (line 30), which does not inspect findings, so a real P1/P2 with one bad field (or an entire findings list of them) becomes findings:[]. That emptied candidate is the critic's sole input (lines 34–38); the critic only prunes and never adds findings, so deriveVerdict (line 43) sees no blocking items and returns pass. Previously the default strict parse aborted the review instead of publishing a false clean result.

findings.title: Do not coerce malformed review output into an empty pass
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously threw on non-object input and on missing/non-string summary or non-array findings/checked/residual_risks. Those throws are replaced with summary "" and empty arrays. Substituting raw=null or raw={} (or findings not an array) now returns {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}. Callers cannot tell a truncated or invalid payload from a real zero-finding review; a missing findings array is stored as [].

findings.title: Do not map malformed review output to empty success
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously threw on non-object input, non-string summary, or non-array findings/checked/residual_risks. Those throws are gone: null, undefined, {}, or a partial object now become { summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] }. That shape is a legitimate empty review, so callers of this exported function can no longer tell a failed/malformed parse from a real no-finding review and will treat the fallback as a successful result.

findings.title: Reject malformed review JSON instead of returning empty success
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is an exported parser. It previously threw on non-object input and on missing/non-string summary or non-array findings/checked/residual_risks. Those throws are gone: raw=null/undefined/5/'nope'/{} all take Array.isArray(raw?.findings) → false and String(raw?.summary ?? '') → '' and return {summary:'', findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}. That shape is a legitimate empty review (no issues). Callers can no longer tell a crashed/garbage model response from a real pass; a public API now forces failure-as-value.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch is still a live public path (on.workflow_dispatch.inputs.pr_number required, job if allows it, --pr still reads the input). That event has no pull_request payload, so github.event.pull_request.head.sha / base.ref / base.sha / head.sha are empty. The deleted else branch used `gh pr view $PR_NUM` to resolve head/base/base_ref; the new expressions instead take github.ref for checkout, default BASE_REF to main, and export empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA. Checkout therefore succeeds on the dispatch branch (not the PR head), so this self-review workflow installs and runs src/cli.ts from the wrong tree, and the review step no longer receives the PR OIDs.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch is still a live path (on.workflow_dispatch, job if, required pr_number, --pr still uses inputs.pr_number), but github.event.pull_request.* is empty on that event. The deleted Resolve PR refs step called gh pr view in that case and fed real head/base/base_ref into checkout and the CLI. The replacement does ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref (the branch selected in the dispatch UI, usually the default branch), BASE_REF: github.event.pull_request.base.ref || 'main', and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA from the empty pull_request payload. Checkout therefore installs and runs src/cli.ts from the wrong commit while --pr still names the requested PR, so a manual run can attribute a review of PR N to the wrong tree. git fetch of hardcoded main also fails on repos whose default/base branch is not main.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still runs on workflow_dispatch (if @24) and still takes inputs.pr_number, but the deleted `gh pr view` fallback was the only path that filled head/base when pull_request is absent. On dispatch, github.event.pull_request.* is empty, so checkout ref becomes github.ref (UI-selected branch, not the PR head), BASE_REF becomes 'main' (not the PR base), and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are empty. Install and src/cli.ts then run on the wrong tree with empty SHAs while --pr still names the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer on git spawnSync
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting maxBuffer makes spawnSync use Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes. On overflow the child is killed (ENOBUFS, status null). git() then throws because status !== 0. runLocal's git(['diff', baseSha, 'HEAD']) is the local-review payload and routinely exceeds 1MiB (lockfiles, generated files, large PRs), so those reviews fail. The sibling gh() helper in this file still sets maxBuffer to 64MiB, so the previous git cap was intentional.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB git maxBuffer to avoid large-diff ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1MiB. runLocal always captures the full `git diff <base> HEAD` through git(), so any patch >1MiB is SIGTERM'd with ENOBUFS (status null). git() treats that as failure and throws, so local review cannot start. The previous 64MiB cap (still present on gh()) was the only thing that made this path work for lockfile/generated/large-feature diffs.

findings.title: Keep review-error check conclusion as failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path still titles the check "Needlefish: review failed" and says the PR did not pass, and it still sets process.exitCode = 1, but it now posts Checks API conclusion "neutral" (was "failure"). GitHub documents required-check successes as success, skipped, and neutral, so a required check named "Needlefish" no longer blocks merge when review() throws. That named check-run is the merge-gate this adapter publishes; the Actions job failure is a different status context and does not restore the old contract.

findings.title: Do not mark the Needlefish check passing when review throws
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path still titles the check 'Needlefish: review failed', says the PR 'did NOT pass', and sets process.exitCode = 1, but postCheck now sends conclusion 'neutral'. GitHub required status checks treat success, skipped, and neutral as passing, so a required 'Needlefish' check no longer blocks merge when review() throws. That is also indistinguishable from needs_human, which already maps to neutral.

findings.title: Keep error check-runs as failure, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path used to POST the Needlefish check-run with conclusion failure. It now posts neutral. GitHub documents success, skipped, and neutral as successful required-check statuses, and treats neutral as success for dependent Actions jobs. This adapter's only merge-blocking signal for a completed review is that same check-run: changes_requested maps to failure while process.exitCode stays 0. After this change, a thrown review() is indistinguishable from needs_human at the conclusion field, so a required Needlefish check (and any job that needs it) can pass even though the summary still says the PR did not pass. exitCode 1 only fails the wrapping Actions job, which cannot be the findings gate because findings already exit 0.

findings.title: Do not install or run PR-head code as the review tool
findings.whyItBreaks: Base kept PR head as untrusted data (`path: target`) and executed `frankekn/needlefish@main` from `path: needlefish`. Head checks out `steps.refs.outputs.head` at the workspace root, runs `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` on that tree (packageManager + lifecycle scripts), then executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts --github --pr …` with `GH_TOKEN`. The job still runs on `self-hosted` and still has `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write`. A same-repo PR can change `src/cli.ts` to forge a passing review/check, or change the lockfile/`packageManager` field to run arbitrary code as the runner user. The job `if` already limited runs to same-repo PRs; the deleted trusted-tool checkout existed specifically because that was not enough. Being the needlefish repo does not make PR head a trusted tool — checkout `main` as the tool and `head` only as the target.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted ref, not the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: Base isolated an untrusted PR tree (`path: target`) from a trusted tool checkout (`frankekn/needlefish@main` at `path: needlefish`), then installed and executed only the trusted tree. Head checks out `steps.refs.outputs.head` at the workspace root, runs `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against that tree, and executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` with `GH_TOKEN` (`pull-requests: write`, `checks: write`) on `runs-on: self-hosted`. A same-repo PR can therefore change `src/cli.ts` / `package.json` and emit its own review/check (the exact bypass the deleted comment described). Worse, `if:` still allows `workflow_dispatch` with no same-repo check, and that path is how fork PRs get reviewed (`workflow_dispatch` bypasses the `pull_request` webhook). Dispatching a fork PR number now runs that fork's install scripts and CLI on a persistent runner with a write token; `actions/checkout@v4` also persists credentials by default into the tree being executed.

The previous split (PR head at path target, frankekn/needlefish@main installed and executed) existed specifically to keep the tool trusted; being the needlefish repo does not require executing the head, because main/base already provided the tool while the PR stayed data-only.

findings.title: Restore severity canonicalization; do not default invalid to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: SEVERITIES.includes now runs on the raw field, so values that previously became P0–P2 via String().trim().toUpperCase() (e.g. "p0", " P0 ") fail the guard and are written as P3. Missing/unknown severity also changed from P1 to P3. normalizeReview maps untyped JSON through this function, so a critical finding is persisted and triaged as low-risk.

findings.title: Restore severity canonicalization; stop rewriting misses as P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is the sanitizer for untyped review JSON (normalizeReview maps any[] through it). The old path did String(raw.severity??'').trim().toUpperCase() then membership, so 'p0', ' P1 ', and 'p2' became P0/P1/P2, and anything else became P1. The new path does SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) with no coerce/trim/case-fold and falls back to P3. Substituting live inputs: 'p0' → includes is false → severity='P3' (was 'P0'); ' P1 ' → P3 (was 'P1'); undefined/''/'nope' → P3 (was 'P1'). A real P3 and a failed parse of P0 are now the same stored value, so callers of the exported Finding contract under-rank or hide high-severity findings.

findings.title: Keep canonicalizing severity so p0/whitespace do not become P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview feeds untyped JSON into normalizeFinding. Previously severity was String(raw).trim().toUpperCase() then allowlisted, so "p0", " P1 ", and "p2" became P0/P1/P2, and missing/garbage defaulted to P1. The new strict includes(raw.severity) rejects those inputs and writes P3. That is wrong classification on the public review contract: a P0 reported as "p0" ships as low-risk P3, and omitted severity is now fail-open instead of P1.

findings.title: Strip GitHub tokens from the Codex spawn environment
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync is now called without `env`, so Node inherits full `process.env` (default). GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN — previously deleted from the child env — are therefore visible to `codex exec` (and to whatever `CODEX_BIN` points at). `-s read-only` only constrains the Codex sandbox; it does not strip process environment. In CI that typically means the job's GITHUB_TOKEN is available to an LLM-driven subprocess that takes untrusted prompt/repo input and can read env (printenv/shell) or call GitHub APIs, which is a credential leak / privilege bypass of the control this diff removes.

findings.title: Do not pass GitHub tokens to the spawned Codex process
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous spawnSync call passed a copy of process.env with GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN deleted. This PR removes that sanitized env, and Node spawnSync defaults env to process.env when the option is omitted. The child is still `codex exec -s read-only`; that sandbox flag does not strip environment variables. Any parent that holds GitHub credentials (typical in Actions via GITHUB_TOKEN, or a local GH_TOKEN) now leaks them into an LLM-driven subprocess that can read env, echo tokens in output, or use `gh`/the GitHub API.

findings.title: Stop leaking GitHub tokens into the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block cloned process.env, removed GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and passed that object as spawnSync's env. spawnSync with no env option defaults to process.env, so those credentials now reach `codex exec`. runCodex is exported, takes an arbitrary prompt, and returns `--output-last-message`; the child can read the tokens, echo them in the returned last message, or use them via gh/git/API. That is a present secret-isolation bypass of the previous denylist, not a speculative future caller.

findings.title: Restore fork-PR guard on self-hosted review job
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only job-level fork check. After removal the `review` job always runs on `pull_request` from forks, on `runs-on: self-hosted`. It then checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` and executes that tree (`pnpm install` lifecycle scripts, then `tsx src/cli.ts`). A fork PR can therefore run arbitrary code on the runner host (credentials, network, later jobs), which the previous predicate rejected.

findings.title: Restore fork-origin guard on self-hosted review job
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control preventing `pull_request` jobs from forks. The job still `runs-on: self-hosted`, checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, runs `pnpm install` (lifecycle scripts), then executes the PR's own `src/cli.ts`. A fork PR can therefore run arbitrary code on the persistent runner host (filesystem, network, and later jobs' credentials). GitHub does not treat `pull_request` from forks as a sandbox for self-hosted runners; `GITHUB_TOKEN` being read-only for forks does not stop that host compromise.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard; fork PRs RCE self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only gate keeping `pull_request` jobs on same-repo heads. After removal, a fork PR still matches `on.pull_request`, is scheduled on `runs-on: self-hosted`, checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, runs `pnpm install` (lifecycle scripts), then executes the PR's own `src/cli.ts`. That is untrusted code execution on a persistent runner (poisoning later privileged jobs). GitHub also forces a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` on fork `pull_request` events, so this does not enable the intended review-write path.

findings.title: Do not treat 0ms as invalid in readRunnerDurationMs
findings.whyItBreaks: The accept predicate changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`. An explicit `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` or `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` is a present finite duration meaning do not wait (next-tick SIGKILL / give-up via setTimeout). It now fails `parsed > 0` and is replaced with the defaults 5000 and 2000, so operators who disabled those waits block for seconds after timeout. Unset input is already handled by the empty/undefined branch at line 133; 0 is not unset.

findings.title: Do not map explicit 0 ms durations to multi-second fallbacks
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs previously returned parsed 0 for finite "0". Both module-load call sites pass that number to setTimeout with no further clamp. NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 therefore scheduled SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM (line 124); NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 called finish() immediately after SIGKILL (line 123). parsed > 0 now classifies 0 as invalid and substitutes fallbacks 5000 and 2000, so those env values no longer disable the waits—they restore the defaults. The exported helper does the same silent substitution for any "0" input.

findings.title: Keep zero as a valid runner duration instead of falling back
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`. `Number("0")` is finite 0, so `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` (and any caller of exported `readRunnerDurationMs("0", fallback)`) now return 5000 and 2000 instead of 0. Those values are `setTimeout` delays after SIGTERM and SIGKILL; 0 previously meant immediate next-tick SIGKILL / give-up. Operators who set 0 to disable those waits now wait seconds, and 0 is indistinguishable from an invalid parse.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage so files outside MAX_HOTSPOTS are reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now deep-reviews only sortByRisk(hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) (MAX_HOTSPOTS=6). The backstop that pushed bundle.changedFiles not in those hotspots into a tail hotspot was removed. isLarge is already true when changedFiles.length > 10, so a live large PR with disjoint hotspot membership leaves paths that never appear in a deep.md {{HOTSPOT}} payload. Those files cannot emit findings or blocking residuals, so review() can PASS without looking at them.

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual_risks instead of hardcoding []
findings.whyItBreaks: Each successful deep pass still returns residual_risks (including blocks:true when evidence is incomplete), but the loop only concatenates findings and candidateMerged sets residual_risks to []. The large-PR critic is then given that JSON plus patchStat only, so dropped blocking residuals cannot be reconstructed. deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) therefore cannot distinguish “deep pass flagged unverifiable” from a clean review and can PASS.

findings.title: Keep a tail hotspot so large PRs deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge still caps the map at MAX_HOTSPOTS=6, but this PR deletes the tail-coverage hotspot that appended every changed file not in those 6. isLarge already fires when changedFiles.length > 10, so files only in dropped hotspots (or never assigned by the map LLM) are never sent to deep.md. Nothing records that gap, so the critic prunes a candidate that omitted them and the published review can PASS while changed files were never deep-reviewed.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual_risks before the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Deep reviews previously forwarded res.residual_risks (and on deep failure, a blocks=true residual naming the unreviewed files) into candidateMerged, which is the critic's input and the only channel those signals had into deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks). The loop no longer collects them and candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded []. A deep pass that could not verify a live path now looks identical to 'no residuals', so the critic/verdict can PASS where the pipeline previously had a blocking gap.

findings.title: Keep substituting critic {{BASE}}/{{HEAD}} with review SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: loadPrompt("critic.md") is unchanged, but both critic builders dropped .replace("{{BASE}}", bundle.baseSha) and .replace("{{HEAD}}", bundle.headSha). deep.md in the same file still interpolates those slots, so that is the template convention. On the large path {{PATCH}} is only patchStat (or a 'repo at head' hint), so the critic no longer receives the commits it needs to ground/prune findings; leftover {{BASE}}/{{HEAD}} tokens are also left in the small-PR critic prompt (lines 59-61).

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage so unmapped files are still deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge still does sortByRisk(hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) with MAX_HOTSPOTS=6. The deleted tail-coverage hotspot was the only path that assigned bundle.changedFiles not in those six surfaces to a deep.md pass. Substituting the new list: field=hotspots value=top-6-only → for (const h of hotspots) @97 → only those files are sent to deep review. Unmapped or overflow files produce no findings, no checked line, and no residual. A large review can look finished while entire changed files were never reviewed.

findings.title: Forward deep residual_risks instead of hardcoding an empty list
findings.whyItBreaks: Successful deep passes used to concatenate res.residual_risks into candidateMerged (and failed passes pushed blocks:true). The merge now always sets residual_risks: []. field=residual_risks value=[] → JSON.stringify(candidateMerged) into critic.md @116 → critic, deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) @122, and ReviewResult.residualRisks @128 all observe an empty list, which is indistinguishable from 'no unresolved risk'. Exported review() can therefore PASS/omit blocking 'could not verify' signals from deep review.

findings.title: Restore focus and deep on the large-PR map and deep prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: review(bundle) still accepts Bundle.focus and Bundle.deep, and reviewSmall still JSON.stringifies the whole bundle into review.md. reviewLarge previously put both fields on mapBundle and substituted bundle.focus ?? "(none)" into deep.md's {{FOCUS}} slot. After this deletion, map JSON is only {baseSha, headSha, patchStat, changedFiles, agentsMd}, and the deep prompt is built with no {{FOCUS}} replacement. On the large path (patch > 30000 chars or > 10 files)—the path that most needs narrowing—operator focus never reaches the map or deep model; if deep.md still contains {{FOCUS}}, that token is left literal.

findings.title: Restore focus interpolation on the large-PR deep pass
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge previously steered each deep pass with .replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)") and also forwarded focus/deep on the map payload. Those writes were deleted and nothing else reads bundle.focus/deep on this path, so a non-null focus never reaches the deep (or map) model. reviewSmall still JSON.stringifies the full bundle, so the same input is honored only under the small-PR threshold. This patch does not update deep.md, so {{FOCUS}} is also left unsubstituted in the prompt.

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution on the large-PR deep prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: review() routes oversized patches to reviewLarge. That path used to replace {{FOCUS}} in prompts/deep.md with bundle.focus ?? "(none)" before runCodex. The replace was deleted; AGENTS/HOTSPOT/BASE/HEAD are still filled, so the template still expects FOCUS. Every large deep call now sends a leftover {{FOCUS}} token instead of the caller-supplied focus (or the explicit "(none)"). reviewSmall still JSON.stringifies the full Bundle, so the same public field works on small PRs and is silently dropped on large ones. Map-pass JSON also no longer includes focus/deep, so hotspot ranking cannot honor focus either.

findings.title: Carry rounded 60s into the next minute in formatDuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are taken from raw ms while seconds are Math.round of the leftover. For leftover in [59500, 59999] that round is 60, so the live stats footer interpolates '60s' (e.g. 59500ms) or '1m 60s' (e.g. 119500ms) instead of '1m 0s' / '2m 0s'. The previous round-total-seconds-then-split path carried that boundary correctly.

findings.title: Carry seconds when remainder rounds to 60
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from ms first, then the leftover `ms % 60000` is rounded to seconds. For any duration with remainder in [59500, 60000) — e.g. 59500, 59999, 119500 — `Math.round` yields 60. The return interpolates that value as-is, so the stats footer prints '60s' or '1m 60s' instead of carrying into '1m 0s' / '2m 0s'. The previous round-then-split path never emitted 60 because `totalSeconds % 60` is always 0–59. Both call sites (`s.durationMs` at line 75 and `result.totalDurationMs` at line 80) embed the string in the review markdown.

findings.title: Carry rounded leftover seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floored from raw ms while seconds is Math.round of the leftover. For any duration in [n*60000+59500, (n+1)*60000), leftover rounds to 60 (JS Math.round(59.5)===60). Substituting that into the format branch: 119500ms → minutes=1, seconds=60 → '1m 60s' (old code: round-to-total-seconds first → '2m 0s'); 59500ms → minutes=0 → '60s' instead of '1m 0s'. Callers at renderMarkdown stats/total concatenate that string into the review markdown.

findings.title: Reject 0 in parsePositiveInteger; 0 is not a positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parser is named parsePositiveInteger and still throws `${label} requires a positive integer`, but the guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`. Zero is therefore returned as valid: `Number('0')===0` and also `Number('')===0` / `Number('   ')===0` / `Number('-0')===-0`. Callers of this public API can no longer distinguish invalid input from a legitimate value and will treat 0 as a positive integer.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger is a public parser whose name and error text promise a strictly positive integer. Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` lets 0 through: `Number.isInteger(0)` is true and `0 < 0` is false, so the function returns 0 instead of throwing. The same bound also accepts strings that coerce to 0 (`""`, `"0"`, `" "`, `"-0"`). Callers that treat the result as a count, timeout, or limit receive a non-positive value that the contract said was invalid.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parser is still named parsePositiveInteger and still throws `${label} requires a positive integer`, but the guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`. Number.isInteger(0) is true and `0 < 0` is false, so '0' now returns 0 instead of throwing. Number('') and Number(' ') are also 0, so blank input now succeeds the same way. Callers that size, time, or count from this result receive a non-positive value the public contract forbids.
